query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The superior creep resistance of the dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is primarily due to the synergistic effect of a low stacking-fault-energy FCC matrix and finely dispersed, high anti-phase-boundary-energy BCC precipitates. Under continuous loading at high temperature, these precipitates act as strong pinning sites that hinder dislocation climb and rearrangement, while favorable lattice misfit promotes a raft‐like evolution of the phases that further stabilizes the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A dual-phase microstructure comprising a continuous FCC matrix with finely dispersed BCC precipitates (or second phase) in the as-fabricated protective coating.
generation.intervention: Introduce a processing step (e.g., controlled heat treatment or thermomechanical processing) designed to modify the precipitate size/distribution without altering the bulk composition to yield either a refined (optimized) or a deliberately coarsened BCC precipitate morphology.
generation.conditions: Creep tests conducted under sustained high temperature and continuous mechanical load that are within the thermal and stress operating boundaries of the coating (i.e., below temperatures where phase coarsening or transformation occurs).
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial stability and spacing between the FCC matrix and BCC precipitates, including the potential formation of rafted or aligned structures under load that effectively block dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under load at high temperature, the low stacking-fault energy of the FCC matrix limits cross-slip and eases dislocation accumulation. Meanwhile, the finely dispersed BCC precipitates, owing to their high anti-phase-boundary energy, impede dislocation climb and promote a raft-like microstructure. Together, these factors slow down the rate of plastic deformation (creep) by increasing the effective obstacles to dislocation movement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline state, coatings with a finely tuned, stable dual-phase microstructure will exhibit a lower steady-state creep strain rate and a delayed onset of tertiary creep, while coatings with coarsened or irregular precipitate distribution will creep faster under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: As-deposited protective coating with an initial FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure prior to any intervention meant to refine precipitate distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under sustained mechanical loads and elevated temperatures up to the limit where the microstructure remains thermally stable and does not undergo unwanted phase changes or coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in creep strain rate and the critical precipitate size/distribution that optimizes resistance remain uncertain until further systematic experimental variation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coating samples: one set subjected to processing that promotes a finer, uniformly distributed BCC precipitate phase within the FCC matrix, and a control set that either remains unprocessed or is subjected to an annealing treatment that coarsens the precipitates. Conduct identical creep tests (constant high temperature and load) on both sets and monitor the creep strain rates and onset of tertiary creep.
measurements: Creep strain rate versus time using high-temperature extensometry or digital image correlation
Microstructural characterization pre- and post-creep (via TEM/SEM) to assess precipitate size/distribution and raft formation
Dislocation density and dynamic recrystallization analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with the refined precipitate distribution do not exhibit a statistically significant lower creep strain rate or a delayed onset of tertiary creep compared to the coarsened control samples, the hypothesis that the optimized FCC/BCC interface microstructure governs creep resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
